text: “Insist on yourself; never imitate.”
Imitation is the easy road.
It asks nothing of your own judgment.
Borrowed opinions arrive ready to wear.
They rarely fit the person wearing them.
To insist on yourself is not to be loud.
It is to check what you actually believe.
Ask of each habit of thought: *whose is this?*
Some answers will surprise you.
Keep what is yours.
Return the rest, politely.
Originality begins as small honesty.
One true sentence at a time.
Where have you been imitating without noticing?
This is the thread behind the book *Learn To Think For Yourself*.
Your own judgment, built daily.
Insist on *your* thinking.
Start small, start today.

text: “He suffers more than necessary, who suffers before it is necessary.”
Most worry is rehearsal for a play that never opens.
The mind performs it anyway.
We pay the cost of a trouble twice.
Once in advance, once if it arrives.
Notice the moment *what if* begins.
That is the thread to pull.
Ask: is this happening, or am I imagining it?
The answer is often quietly freeing.
Prepare for what you can.
Then set the rest down.
Calm is not the absence of problems.
It is refusing to invoice yourself early.
What are you suffering in advance this week?
This is the thread behind the book *The 14-Day Clarity Reset*.
A short reset for a busy mind.
Pay for trouble *once.*
If it comes at all.

text: “Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.”
Before any theory there was a child asking *why.*
Wonder came first.
Adults often trade wonder for certainty.
Certainty is more comfortable.
Wonder is simply attention without a verdict.
It asks and waits.
Try it on your own thoughts.
*Why did I say that to myself just now?*
Your inner voice is worth being curious about.
It is the narrator of every day.
Listening with wonder changes the tone.
Harsh judges become interesting subjects.
What inside you could you meet with wonder today?
This is the thread behind the book *The Science of Learning Your Inner Speech*.
Curiosity about your own inner voice.
Begin in *wonder.*
Then listen closely.

caption:
Nothing is so firmly believed as what is least known.

text: “Nothing is so firmly believed as what is least known.”
Certainty and knowledge are not the same thing.
Often they are opposites.
The less we have examined a belief,
the less we feel any need to.
Familiar ideas sound true because they are familiar.
Repetition is a quiet persuader.
Try this: pick a belief you hold firmly.
Write what you actually know about it.
The gap between those two is useful.
That gap is where thinking starts.
You do not have to drop the belief.
You only have to *know* it.
Which firm belief of yours has the least behind it?
This is the thread behind the book *Learn To Think For Yourself*.
Examine before you defend.
Know what you *believe.*
And why.
